title.en: Sirius and Canopus: The Grandmother's Rejoicing Song
title.zh: 天狼與老人星：祖母之歡歌

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Sirius and Canopus'

summary.en: Ttuai-an used to rejoice about Canopus when it rose, singing 'Sirius! Sirius! Winks like Canopus! Canopus winks like Sirius!' — while she felt that food was abundant; the stars' winking back and forth is the sign of the good season.
summary.zh: 圖亞安每於老人星升時歡慶，歌曰「天狼！天狼！眨眼如老人星！老人星眨眼如天狼！」——其時她覺食物豐盈；二星互眨乃豐季之兆。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My (step)grandmother, Ttuai-an, was the one who used to rejoice about Canopus. She said — 'Sirius! Sirius! Winks like Canopus! Canopus Winks like Sirius!... Sirius Winks like Canopus!' while my grandmother felt that food was abundant.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 231-233 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the editor's notes: we are wont to say \hu, when food is abundant; the two stars are called by name as they rise, and the song is one of the old people's rejoicing at the beginning of the good season.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 233 notes; not verbatim.

title.en: The Song Sung by the Star \gaunu and by Bushman Women

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'A Song sung by the Star \gaunu, and especially by Bushman Women'

summary.en: 'Does the \garraken flower open? The +ku-yam is the one which opens. Dost thou open? The +ku-yam is the one which opens.' The star \gaunu sings it, and Bushman women sing it especially as they dig bulbs; the riddling call is the star's question and the women's answer.
summary.zh: 「加拉克花開否？開者乃+庫雅姆。爾開否？開者乃+庫雅姆。」此歌星加烏奴唱之，掘球根之桑婦尤歌之；謎語之呼喚，乃星之問與婦之答。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Does the \garraken flower open? The +ku-yam is the one which opens. Dost thou open? The +ku-yam is the one which opens.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 231 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the notes: the \garraken are bulbs, which the Bushmen dig out; \ku-yam is the daisy-like flower in blossom at Mowbray in August; the star \gaunu sings this song, and Bushman women especially sing it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 231 notes; not verbatim.

title.en: The Song of the Caama Fox: Crosser of the Spoor

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1873 by !A!kunta (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Song of the Caama Fox'

summary.en: The caama fox sings 'Crosser of the Spoor! Crosser of the Spoor!' — for it avoids the dog nicely when the dog chases it, turning suddenly to run back across the dog's spoor while the dog races on in front, thinking to catch the fox.
summary.zh: 狐自歌「踏跡者！踏跡者！」——因犬逐之，牠巧妙避讓，急轉回越犬之跡；而犬奔於前，自以為能捕之。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by !A!kunta to Bleek and Lloyd, 1873; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Crosser of the Spoor, Crosser of the Spoor, Crosser of the Spoor, Crosser of the Spoor!
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 223 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the narrator's note: the Caama Fox is called 'Crosser of the Spoor', because it avoids the dog nicely when the dog chases it, and, turning suddenly, runs back, crossing the dog's spoor behind it, while the dog is racing on in front, thinking to catch the Caama Fox by so doing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 223 note; not verbatim.

title.en: The Songs of the Blue Crane

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1879 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Songs of the Blue Crane'

summary.en: The Blue Crane — once a person of the early race and the Mantis's sister — sings about her shoulder, where the krieboom berries lie; she sings 'a splinter of stone which is white' as she runs from a man, sings the walk of peace as she leaves, and sings 'scrape the springbok skin for the bed' as she flaps her wings.
summary.zh: 藍鶴——本為早期之民，螳螂之姊——歌其肩上之克裏布姆漿果；奔逃時歌「白色石片」，離去時歌和平之步，振翅時歌「刮羚皮為床」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San songs dictated by ||kabbo and /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: It is the Blue Crane's story which it sings; it sings about its shoulder, namely, that the 'krieboom' berries are upon its shoulder; it goes along singing — 'The berries are upon my shoulder, The berries are upon my shoulder, The berry it is upon my shoulder.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 225 (public domain).

passages.text: 2. (When running away from a man.) 'A splinter of stone which is white, A splinter of stone which is white.' 3. (When walking slowly, leaving the place — walk of peace.) 'A white stone splinter.' 4. (When it flaps its wings.) 'Scrape the springbok skin for the bed.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 226-227 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the notes: the Blue Crane was formerly a person of the early race; the crane sings about its head, which is shaped like a stone knife and has white feathers; the Bushmen make beds from springbok and goat skins.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 224-227 notes; not verbatim.

title.en: ||kabbo's Song on the Loss of His Tobacco Pouch

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '||kabbo's Song on the Loss of his Tobacco Pouch'

summary.en: 'Famine it is, Famine is here' — the old man's song on his tobacco-hunger: a hungry dog named Blom had come in the night and carried off his pouch, and he woke in the dark and missed it; the little song turns hunger into verse.
summary.zh: 「飢也，飢在此」——老人失煙袋之歌：名布隆之餓犬夜來奪袋；他暗中醒覺，尋而不得；小歌化飢為詩。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by /Han≠kass'o (for ||kabbo) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Famine it is, Famine it is, Famine is here. Famine it is, Famine it is, Famine is here. Famine ['tobacco-hunger' is meant here] — he did not smoke, because a dog had come in the night and carried off from him his pouch. And he arose in the night, he missed his pouch. And then he again lay down, while he did not smoke.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 235-236 (public domain).

passages.text: And we were early seeking for the pouch. We did not find the pouch.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 236 (public domain).

title.en: Stories That Float Like the Wind: ||kabbo's Return
title.zh: 如風漂至之故事：卡布之歸

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1873-1875 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '||kabbo's intended Return Home'

summary.en: Waiting for the moon to turn back for him, ||kabbo plans to go home to listen to the stories: 'I am one who listens behind me... a story is like the wind; it comes from a far-off quarter, and we feel it.' Our names float to places our bodies cannot; the people at home visit each other's huts to sit smoking and hear the histories.
summary.zh: 卡布待月回圓以歸家聽故事：「我乃於背後傾聽者……故事如風，自遠方而來，吾等感之。」吾名能漂至軀體不能至之地；鄉人相訪各屋，對坐吸煙而聽史。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San personal narrative dictated by ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd, 1873-1875; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Thou knowest that I sit waiting for the moon to turn back for me, that I may return to my place... That I may listen to all the people's stories, when I visit them... They are those which they thus tell, they are listening to them; while the other \xe-ssho-\kui (the sun) becomes a little warm, that I may sit in the sun.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 299-301 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: I am here; I do not obtain stories; because I do not visit, so that I might hear stories which float along... For, I am wont to listen, watching for a story, which I want to hear; while I sit waiting for it; that it may float into my ear. These are those to which I am listening with all my ears; while I feel that I sit silent. I must wait (listening) behind me, while I listen along the road; while I feel that my name floats along the road.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 302-303 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: While I feel that a story is the wind. It (the story) is wont to float along to another place. Then, our names do pass through those people; while they do not perceive our bodies go along. For, our names are those which, floating, reach a different place... [||kabbo explains that] a story is 'like the wind, it comes from a far-off quarter, and we feel it.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 304-305 with editor's note (public domain), minor elisions.

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'How \Han≠kass'o's pet Leveret was killed'

summary.en: Tsatsi caught a leveret for the boy, who played with it while it ran; his mother wished him to kill and roast it, he would not, so she sent him to fetch water and killed it while he was gone. They calmed his crying by telling him the lizard's song — the story of the Death of the \khau.
summary.zh: 察特西為少年捕幼兔；兔奔而童追之戲；母欲其殺而炙之，他不從，母遂遣其取水，趁其離去殺兔。眾以蜥蜴之歌——哈之死之故事——安其啼。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San personal memory dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Tsatsi was the one who caught hold of and took up a leveret on the hunting-ground; and, he brought it home alive, he came and gave it to me. And I played with it; I set it down, it ran; I also ran after it... |xabbi-an wished that I should leave off playing with the leveret, that I should kill it, that I should lay it to roast. I was not willing to kill the leveret.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 318-319 (public domain).

passages.text: I was not willing to kill the leveret, because I felt that nothing acted as prettily as it did, when it was gently running, gently running along... Then they told me to fetch water; for I was one who quickly came away from the water... And I went to fetch water; then, they killed my leveret for me, while I was at the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 320 (public domain).

passages.text: Then I came and cried, about it; because I had thought that they would let my leveret alone... They had killed it for me. Therefore, I came and cried... They said, that we should not again get another leveret... Therefore, they soothingly calmed me with the (story of the) lizard; while they wished that I might quietly listen to them.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 320-321 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Bushmen's Letters Are in Their Bodies

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1873 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Bushman Presentiments'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §99

summary.en: 'The Bushmen's letters are in their bodies. They speak, they move, they make their bodies move.' The tapping of the flesh tells of visitors coming (an old wound taps at the place where the wounded man walks), of springbok behind the Brinkkop, of blood soon to flow down the hunter's calves; only fools disobey the body's letters — such as get killed by lions.
summary.zh: 「桑人之書信在其體內。彼等言、動、令其體而動。」肉之搏跳告知來客（舊傷在彼行處而跳）、告知布林山後之羚、告知獵者腿肚將流之血；愚者不從體信者遭獅噬。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San presentiment-lore dictated by ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd, 1873; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Bushmen's letters are in their bodies. They (the letters) speak, they move, they make their (the Bushmen's) bodies move. They order the others to be silent; a man is altogether still, when he feels that his body is tapping (inside). A dream speaks falsely, it is (a thing) which deceives. The presentiment is that which speaks the truth.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 331 (public domain).

passages.text: The beatings tell those who understand them, which way they are not to go, and which arrow they had better not use, and also warn them, when many people are coming to the house on a wagon. They inform people where they can find the person of whom they are in search, i.e., which way they must go to seek him successfully.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 331 with editor's quote of Bleek 1875 §99 (public domain).

passages.text: With regard to an old wound, a Bushman feels a tapping at the wound's place, while the tapping feels that the man (who has the old wound) walks, moving his body... he says to the children: 'Look ye around, for grandfather, for grandfather seems to be coming; this is why I feel the place of his body's old wound.'... He feels a tapping at his ribs; he says to the children: 'The springbok seem to be coming... Climb ye the Brinkkop standing yonder, that ye may look around at all the places. For I feel the springbok sensation.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 332-333 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: I am wont to feel thus, I feel a sensation in the calves of my legs when the springbok's blood is going to run down them. For I always feel blood, when I am about to kill springbok... The other agrees with him (saying): 'Yes, my brother.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 334-335 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Earth Thrown Up by a Fainting Man

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'A Bushman, becoming faint from the Sun's heat when returning home, throws earth into the air'

summary.en: The sun-killed hunter, too spent to reach home, throws earth into the air; the watching wife sees the dust, and the people run out crying 'His heart is that for which he throws up earth; the sun is killing him; give him water quickly!' He sits in the water's coolness while the sun's darkness is removed from his face.
summary.zh: 為日所殺之獵者，力竭難歸，乃據地擲塵上天；守望之妻見之，眾人奔出呼曰「彼擲塵為其心；日殺之；速予水！」。坐於水涼處，日之暗影遂離其面。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San practice-lore dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: A man is wont, when returning home, when he feels as if he should not reach home, he throws up earth (into the air), because he wishes that the people at home may perceive the dust... She stands up, she looks around. And, as she stands looking around, she perceives the dust, she exclaims: 'A person seems to be throwing up earth there!'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 385-386 (public domain).

passages.text: And the people run, run out of the house, exclaiming: 'His heart is that on account of which he throws up earth. Ye must run quickly, that ye may go to give him water quickly; for, it is his heart; the sun is killing him... Ye must quickly go to give him water.'... They go, pouring (water), to cool the man with water. And he first sits up, to remove the darkness from his face; for, the sun's darkness resembles night.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 386-387 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Treatment of Bones: Tsatsi's Way

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '|Nanna-sse. Second Part: the Treatment of Bones'

summary.en: Gnawed bones are poured down at a heap opposite the hut's mouth; the women may not eat the springbok's shoulder blades, for they respect the men's arrows; the dogs may not crunch the bones of the man who shot, or his first finger will be wounded when he shoots; and Tsatsi sews his first finger into a cover to pull the string.
summary.zh: 啃畢之骨傾於屋門前之堆；婦女不得食跳羚肩胛，以敬男子之箭；犬不得嚼射者之骨，否則其食指於射時受傷；察特西縫食指於皮套以挽弓弦。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San custom dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: They (the Bushmen) put the things' bones nicely aside, while they do not throw them about. They put down the bones opposite to the entrance to the hut... they go, they pour down the bones at it. Therefore, they call it, 'The heap of meat bones.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 274 (public domain).

passages.text: The women do not eat (the meat of) the springbok's shoulder blades, because they show respect for the men's arrows, so that the men may quietly kill... Therefore, we do not allow the little children to play upon the springbok skin. For the springbok is wont to get into our flesh, and we become ill.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 277 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the narrator's account of Tsatsi: my grandfather put away in the sticks of the hut the upper bones of the fore leg, the shoulder blades and the springbok's \khuru-\khuruken, because the first finger of the shooting hand gets a wound when we shoot if the dogs eat the springboks' bones; we sew the first finger into a cover, which the wife cuts out and sews for us, and then we pull the bow-string while we feel that our finger is inside.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 282-283; not verbatim.

title.en: The \goih-\goih: Bullroarer for the Bees and the Night Dance

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The use of the \goih\goih, followed by an Account of a Bushman Dance'

summary.en: The \goih-\goih is beaten so the bees may grow abundant and drift into other people's places, that honey may be cut; the men bring the honey to the hungry women at home, the women make the drum, and the dance goes round till sunrise — the men dancing and the women clapping, the drum-dust rising upon every face.
summary.zh: 擊牛鳴器使蜂繁衍、飄入他家之域，以得割蜜；男子攜蜜歸予飢餓之家婦；婦製鼓，眾舞至日出——男舞女拍，鼓塵揚於眾面。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San practice-lore dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The people beat the \goih\goih, (in order) that the bees may become abundant for the people, (in order) that the bees may go into the other people's places, that the people may eat honey... And the people take honey to the women at home. For, the women are dying of hunger, at home... that the women may go to eat... while they wish that the women may make a drum for them, so that they may dance, when the women are satisfied with food.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 353-355 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: Then, the sun rises, while they are dancing there, while they feel that they are satisfied with food... Therefore, the sun shines upon the backs of their heads; while the women get the dust of the drum... their foot's dust covers the women's faces; because they have danced strongly... Therefore they sleep, letting the sun set; because they are tired when they have been dancing there.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 355-357 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: \hara and \tao: The Black Head of the Handsome Young Man

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '\hara and \tao'

summary.en: \hara is black and anoints the head; \tao is red and rubs the body. The head anointed with \hara shimmers; and the old women say of a youth: 'That man, he is a handsome young man, on account of his head's blackness, which is surpassingly beautiful with the \hara's blackness — his head is like the \khi tree.'
summary.zh: 赫拉為黑，塗於首；陶為赤，擦於身。以赫拉塗之首閃爍；老嫗謂少年曰：「此人因首之黑而為美男——其黑至美；其首如克希樹。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San practice-lore dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: \hara is black; the people having mixed it with fat anoint their heads with it; while \tao is red, and the people rub their bodies with it, when they have pounded it... They anoint their heads very nicely, while they wish that their head's hair may descend. And it becomes abundant on account of it... wishing that the hair may grow downwards, that their heads may become black with blackness.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 375 (public domain).

passages.text: \hara sparkles; therefore, our heads shimmer, on account of it... Therefore, the Bushmen are wont to say, when the old women are talking there: 'That man, he is a handsome young man, on account of his head, which is surpassingly beautiful with the \hara's blackness.' They say, 'Handsome young man' to him, 'His head is surpassingly beautiful; for, his head is like the \khi tree.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 376-378 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: Doings of the Springbok: Mothers, Kids and the Hunter's Warning
title.zh: 跳羚之為：母子與獵者之警

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Doings of the Springbok'

summary.en: The mother springbok grunts 'a, a, a' as she trots with her kid, and the kid bleats 'me, me, me'; the herd makes a resounding noise because they are many. The hunter, lying hidden, warns: 'O beast of prey! thou art the one who hearest the place behind — the male springbok which stand around will go along, passing behind you; because I am lying down, and they do not perceive me.'
summary.zh: 羚母負子而行，喉中作「阿，阿，阿」；幼者啼「米，米，米」；群聲迴響，因其眾多。匿伏獵者警曰：「猛獸啊！爾所聞者乃身後之地——周圍之公羚將自爾身後經過；因我臥伏，彼等不見我。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San observation-lore dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The mother springbok is wont to do thus, as she trots along, when she has a springbok kid which is little, she grunts, as she trots along; she says — 'a, a, a'... while the springbok kids also cry (bleat), while their mothers cry (grunt). Their mothers say — 'a, a, a,' the springbok kids say — 'me, me, me'... Therefore, we are wont to say: 'O beast of prey! thou art the one who hearest the place behind, it is resonant with sound.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 244-246 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: For these male springbok which stand around, are those which will go along, passing behind you; because I am lying down, and they do not perceive me; they will have to go along, passing behind you, when ye have gone behind the hill... while the place is resonant with sound.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 246 (public domain).
